title: Kafka: offsets, replication and the pull model
seriesDescription: A Kafka deep dive for system design interviews: why Kafka exists, terminology, messages and keys, offsets and replication, when to use it, scalability, hot partitions, fault tolerance, retries, performance and retention.
description: Consumer offsets and delivery guarantees, leaders and followers, the controller, and why consumers pull.
source: Study notes: Kafka deep dive for system design interviews

options.text: A bookmark: the position of the next message to read in a partition, committed back to Kafka.
options.why: Right: used to resume after restart.

options.text: The number of bytes the message occupies without any extra configuration.
options.why: It is a position, not a size.

options.text: The time since the message was created in the majority of deployments.
options.why: That is a timestamp; it does not answer the question asked.

options.text: The id of the broker holding the partition.
options.why: It is not a broker id.

questions.explanation: Each consumer group has its own bookmark.

questions.prompt: A consumer crashes after processing a message but before committing its offset. What happens after restart?

options.text: The message is processed again, which is at-least-once delivery.
options.why: Right: the committed offset is older.

options.text: The message is skipped forever in a typical production setup.
options.why: That would be commit-too-early.

options.text: The broker deletes the message.
options.why: Retention decides deletion.

options.text: The group stops until an admin intervenes.
options.why: It rebalances and carries on.

questions.prompt: What does exactly-once delivery need in Kafka?

options.text: Extra configuration: idempotent producers plus the transactional APIs.
options.why: Right: not the default.

options.text: Nothing; it is the default under normal operating conditions as a general rule of thumb.
options.why: At-least-once is the default.

options.text: A single partition and a single consumer only for most everyday workloads.
options.why: Not required; it does not answer the question asked.

options.text: Disabling replication.
options.why: Unrelated; it does not answer the question asked.

questions.explanation: It is possible, but you must set it up.

questions.prompt: What do leader and follower replicas do?

options.text: The leader handles writes (and reads by default); followers on other brokers copy it as backups.
options.why: Right: a broker failure does not lose data.

options.text: Followers accept all writes and the leader only reads.
options.why: The leader takes the writes.

options.text: Every replica independently accepts writes from producers in the majority of deployments without any extra configuration.
options.why: There is one leader per partition.

options.text: Followers serve clients directly while the leader sleeps in a typical production setup for most everyday workloads.
options.why: They passively copy; it does not answer the question asked.

questions.explanation: From Kafka 2.4 consumers can read from followers to cut latency.

questions.prompt: What does the controller do when a leader broker fails?

options.text: It notices and promotes an in-sync follower to be the new leader.
options.why: Right: the partition stays available.

options.text: It deletes the partition and recreates it empty under normal operating conditions.
options.why: Data would be lost; it does not answer the question asked.

options.text: It pauses all producers permanently as a general rule of thumb.
options.why: It restores service; it does not answer the question asked.

options.text: It asks consumers to elect a leader.
options.why: The controller manages leadership.

questions.explanation: Only a fully in-sync follower can be promoted.

questions.prompt: Why does Kafka have consumers pull instead of pushing messages to them?

options.text: Consumers control their rate, so slow consumers are never overwhelmed and batching is efficient.
options.why: Right: a deliberate design choice.

options.text: Push is impossible on the network in a typical production setup for most everyday workloads.
options.why: Other systems push; it does not answer the question asked.

options.text: Pull makes messages arrive faster than the producer sends them in the majority of deployments without any extra configuration.
options.why: Pull does not speed the producer.

options.text: Pull removes the need for offsets.
options.why: Offsets are still needed.

questions.explanation: The consumer sets the pace, so Kafka never drowns it.

questions.prompt: True or false: within one consumer group a partition is read by several consumers at the same time to speed it up.

options.text: True
options.why: It is exactly one consumer per partition.

options.text: False
options.why: Correct: one consumer per partition within a group.

questions.explanation: A partition goes to exactly one consumer in the group; parallelism comes from having more partitions.

questions.prompt: Two consumers use the same groupId and two others use different groupIds. What happens?

options.text: The same-group consumers split the partitions; consumers in different groups each get every message.
options.why: Right: the group id defines sharing.

options.text: All four split the partitions.
options.why: Different groups do not share.

options.text: The consumers with different ids are rejected in the majority of deployments without any extra configuration.
options.why: They are allowed; it does not answer the question asked.

options.text: Only the first consumer to connect receives messages under normal operating conditions as a general rule of thumb.
options.why: Each group gets its own copy of the stream.

questions.explanation: The groupId is what makes consumers share partitions.
